intro/hello: Welcome to convolutional networks, the architecture that taught computers to see.
intro/flat: So far, every network has read an image as one long row of numbers.
intro/wired: Each number is wired to every neuron, so a pixel and its neighbor mean no more to each other than two opposite corners.
intro/big: It is also expensive. A modest two hundred by two hundred color photo needs a hundred and twenty million weights for a layer of a thousand neurons.
intro/keep: Convolutional networks keep the neurons, the loss and backpropagation. They change only the wiring, in two ways.
intro/patch: Each neuron looks at a small patch of the image.
intro/share: And the same weights are reused everywhere, so an edge detector works wherever the edge is.
intro/payoff: That cuts the weights by orders of magnitude, and it is why conv nets took over computer vision.
volumes/block: Conv nets arrange their neurons the way an image is arranged: in a block, with a width, a height and a depth.
volumes/cifar: A see-far ten image is thirty two by thirty two by three: one slice each for red, green and blue.
volumes/word: Careful: depth here means channels, not layers.
volumes/contract: Every layer takes a volume in, and hands a new volume on.
volumes/conv: A convolution layer with twelve filters makes twelve activation maps: thirty two by thirty two by twelve.
volumes/relu: A ray-loo zeroes the negatives. Same size, no weights.
volumes/pool: Pooling halves the width and height, to sixteen by sixteen by twelve.
volumes/fc: And a fully connected layer turns what is left into ten class scores.
volumes/weights: Only the convolution and fully connected layers have weights to learn. Now let us open up the convolution layer.
slide/own: A convolution layer owns a set of small filters. Start simple: one three by three filter on a grayscale image.
slide/hand: This one is made by hand: minus ones on the left, plus ones on the right.
slide/lay: Lay it over a patch of the image, multiply each weight by the pixel under it, and add up all nine products.
slide/match: That number says how well the patch matches the filter. Dark on the left and bright on the right gives a big answer.
slide/slide: Now slide the filter one step and do it again, along every row and down every column.
slide/pad: A ring of zeros around the border keeps the output at thirty two by thirty two.
slide/map: The result is an activation map. It responds wherever brightness changes from left to right: a vertical edge detector.
slide/relu: After a ray-loo, only the positive responses survive.
slide/other: Other numbers make other detectors: horizontal edges, a blur, a sharpen.
slide/learn: A conv net learns its own, and its first filters end up looking much like these: edges at many angles, and blobs of color.
depth/depth: Real inputs have depth, and a filter always reaches through all of it.
depth/size: A typical first layer filter is five by five by three: five pixels square, and all three colors deep.
depth/field: Each output number is a neuron that sees only this small region, its receptive field. That is seventy five weights and a bias.
depth/deep: Deeper in, a three by three filter on twenty channels has a hundred and eighty: small in space, but full depth.
depth/sum: Written out, one output is a triple sum over the filter's rows, columns and channels, plus a bias.
depth/loops: Three sigmas are three nested loops. In NumPy: multiply two same-shaped blocks, and sum.
depth/stride: The stride, S, only decides where each block starts.
depth/demo: Here it is for real: a five by five by three input padded with zeros, and two three by three by three filters at stride two.
depth/one: Each output is twenty seven products: three slice sums, plus the bias.
depth/jump: The window jumps two cells at a time, and nine positions fill the first map.
depth/second: The second filter revisits the same windows with different weights.
depth/column: The numbers stacked at one position see the same patch through different filters: a depth column.
size/three: Three settings decide the size of a convolution layer's output.
size/K: Depth, K, is the number of filters, one activation map each.
size/S: Stride, S, is how far the filter jumps. Stride two skips every other position.
size/P: Padding, P, is how many rings of zeros go around the input.
size/row: Look at a single row of width N, and a filter of width three.
size/slide: The filter can start at zero, one, two, three or four. Its left edge travels four steps, so there are five positions.
size/two: At stride two, it lands on zero, two and four. Four over two, plus one: three positions.
size/formula: Padding just widens the row first. So the output width is N minus F plus two P, over S, plus one.
size/bad: If that division is not even, the setting is invalid: at stride three, the last placement hangs off the edge.
size/same: The favorite is same padding: P equals F minus one, over two, and the output stays exactly as wide as the input.
size/alex: AlexNet, the 2012 ImageNet winner, read two twenty seven by two twenty seven images with ninety six eleven by eleven filters at stride four.
size/alex2: Two twenty seven minus eleven, over four, plus one, is fifty five. So the output is fifty five by fifty five by ninety six.
sharing/naive: Count that layer naively: fifty five by fifty five by ninety six neurons, each with three sixty three weights and a bias.
sharing/total: That is over a hundred and five million parameters, for one layer.
sharing/assume: The way out is an assumption that suits images: a filter useful in one place is useful everywhere. An edge is an edge, top or bottom.
sharing/share: So every neuron in one activation map shares a single filter.
sharing/count: Ninety six filters, plus their biases, is about thirty five thousand parameters.
sharing/ratio: That is three thousand and twenty five times fewer, one for each position, and the image size no longer matters.
sharing/name: Sliding one shared filter over an input is a convolution: hence the name.
sharing/grad: In backprop, every position adds its gradient into the one shared filter.
sharing/numpy: In NumPy, each output is a slice of the input times a filter, summed, plus a bias.
sharing/steps: Each step along a map moves the slice by the stride: zero to five, two to seven, four to nine.
sharing/map1: The second map reuses the same slices with a different filter.
sharing/local: Sharing can be wrong. If every input is a centered face, eyes always sit near the top, and each place deserves its own weights: a locally connected layer.
more/cols: Those loops are slow. Real libraries copy each receptive field into a column of one big matrix: a trick called im to col.
more/rows: Each filter becomes one row of a second matrix.
more/mm: Then the whole layer is one fast matrix multiply, paid for in memory, since overlapping patches get copied.
more/back: Its backward pass is a convolution too: the upstream gradient, against the same filters, flipped.
more/one: A one by one filter sounds pointless, until you remember that it spans the full depth.
more/one2: On sixty four channels, it is a dot product at every pixel. Thirty two of them make the volume thirty two deep.
more/one3: It mixes channels without looking at neighbors: a cheap way to change depth.
more/dil: Dilated convolutions spread a filter's taps apart. With a gap of one, three taps cover five cells, with only three weights.
more/dil3: Stack layers whose taps sit one, two, then four cells apart, and the reach grows from three, to seven, to fifteen: exponentially, not linearly.
pooling/what: Between convolution layers, networks often insert a pooling layer. It shrinks the width and height, saving computation and curbing overfitting.
pooling/slice: It works on each depth slice separately.
pooling/max: The usual form is max pooling, two by two at stride two: keep the largest of every four numbers.
pooling/run: Six wins the first window. Then eight, three, and four.
pooling/halve: Width and height halve, depth stays, and three quarters of the numbers are gone.
pooling/ask: It asks each window: did this feature fire strongly anywhere in here? And it forgets where.
pooling/settings: There are no weights. Besides two by two, only the overlapping three by three at stride two is common.
pooling/back: Going backward, the gradient of a max flows entirely to the winner: nudging a loser changes nothing.
pooling/switch: So the forward pass remembers where each maximum was. Those positions are the switches.
pooling/route: Each incoming gradient goes straight to its switch, and the other three cells get zero.
pooling/avg: Average pooling would split it four ways instead. In practice, max has worked better.
pooling/rid: Some networks drop pooling entirely, and shrink with an occasional stride two convolution layer instead.
fc/norm: Early conv nets also had normalization layers, but they added little, and fell out of use.
fc/fc: Fully connected layers you know: every neuron sees the whole input, and the layer is one matrix multiply.
fc/disguise: The twist: an FC layer is a convolution layer in disguise.
fc/same: Take four thousand and ninety six neurons reading a seven by seven by five twelve volume. Reshape each one's weights into that same shape: a filter as big as its input.
fc/fits: It fits in exactly one position, so the convolution layer outputs the very same numbers.
fc/why: Why bother? Because the convolution version can slide over a bigger image.
fc/alex: An AlexNet style network shrinks a two twenty four pixel image to seven by seven, then three FC layers make the scores. Convert all three to convolutions.
fc/big: Now feed it a three eighty four pixel image. The features come out twelve by twelve, and the seven by seven filter fits at six positions each way.
fc/grid: Out comes a six by six grid of scores, one for every two twenty four pixel crop, thirty two pixels apart.
fc/cheap: One pass equals thirty six runs of the original network, at a fraction of the cost.
arch/pattern: Most conv nets follow one pattern: a few convolution and ray-loo layers, then a pool, repeated until the image is small, then a few fully connected layers.
arch/deeper: Bigger networks put two or three convolutions before each pool, building richer features before pooling throws detail away.
arch/l1: They also prefer small filters. Stack three three by three layers: a neuron in the first sees three by three pixels.
arch/l2: One in the second sees three by three of those, which reach five by five pixels.
arch/l3: The third reaches seven by seven: as far as one big seven by seven filter.
arch/relus: But the stack has three ray-loos instead of one, so its features are more expressive.
arch/params: And it has fewer weights: with C channels, twenty seven C squared for the stack, against forty nine C squared for the big filter.
arch/rules: Rules of thumb: three by three convolutions at stride one with same padding keep the size, and two by two max pools do the shrinking.
arch/hero: And from 2016: don't be a hero. Take a network that works well on ImageNet, download its weights, and fine tune it on your data.
cases/lenet: A few networks mark the milestones, starting in the 1990s with Le Net, which read zip codes and digits.
cases/score: The score is ImageNet's top five error: how often the right label is missing from a network's five best guesses.
cases/alex: In 2012, AlexNet won with about sixteen percent, against twenty six for the runner up: a bigger, deeper Le Net, trained on two GPUs.
cases/recipe: Its recipe became the template: ray-loo, dropout, momentum, and a learning rate cut by ten whenever progress stalled.
cases/zf: In 2013, Z F net retuned it.
cases/vgg: In 2014, V G G net showed that depth matters: sixteen layers of just three by three convolutions and pools, with a hundred and thirty eight million parameters.
cases/goog: The winner, Google net, ran small filters side by side, with one by one convolutions keeping it to a few million parameters.
cases/res: In 2015, ResNet added each block's input back to its output, so each block only learns a correction.
cases/res2: That made a hundred and fifty two layers trainable, and cut the error to three point six percent.
memory/limit: The tightest constraint is usually memory. In 2016, a typical GPU had three to six gigabytes.
memory/three: Memory goes to activations, to parameters, and to odds and ends like the images themselves.
memory/acts: Training keeps every layer's activations for backprop, plus a gradient of the same size.
memory/params: Parameters come with their gradients and a momentum cache: about three copies.
memory/vgg: Here is VGG sixteen, layer by layer.
memory/early: Activations live mostly in the first few convolution layers, where the volumes are big: about fifteen million numbers per image.
memory/late: Weights live mostly in the fully connected layers: the first one alone holds over a hundred million.
memory/total: At four bytes each and a batch of sixty four, that is about eight point eight gigabytes.
memory/batch: The activations grow with the batch and the weights do not, so when a network does not fit, shrink the batch.
outro/stack: So, a conv net is a stack of layers that turn one volume into another.
outro/conv: Convolution layers slide small, full depth filters over their input, and sharing makes them cheap.
outro/size: N minus F plus two P, over S, plus one, gives the size of what comes out.
outro/pool: Pooling shrinks, and routes gradients through its switches.
outro/fc: Fully connected layers are convolutions with filters as big as their input.
outro/arch: Good networks stack small filters, with their memory in early activations and their parameters in late layers.
outro/next: Next, the interactive chapter: slide filters over real images, step through a convolution, and break the size formula yourself.
